name: Hot-Hand Fallacy
description: People may believe someone on a success streak is more likely to keep succeeding. The catch is that this belief is not simply 'wrong' in every domain: some streak perceptions are illusory, but some hot-hand performance is real.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to sports, gaming, creator, marketplace, and experimentation products that surface streaks or momentum signals. Designers can accidentally reinforce bad randomness intuitions, or overcorrect and deny genuine momentum where it exists.
myth_risk_note: Miller & Sanjurjo (2018) demonstrated a hidden statistical selection-bias error in the classic 1985 hot-hand study; correcting for it reveals a real, statistically significant hot-hand effect in the original data, and independent MLB evidence (Green & Zwiebel 2017) corroborates real streak phenomena. The textbook 'fallacy' framing overstates what the corrected evidence actually shows.
prevalence_note: Widely recognized in sports, gaming, betting, and streak-based product discussions. Less universal than gambler's fallacy in general UX teaching, but far from obscure.

findings.description: Across four controlled shooting experiments, repeated sessions over time, and improved statistical tests, Miller and Sanjurjo found strong evidence that genuine hot-hand performance exists both across datasets and within individuals. Expert observers in a companion belief study could also successfully predict which shooters were getting hottest.
findings.source_title: A Cold Shower for the Hot Hand Fallacy: Robust Evidence from Controlled Settings

findings.description: The classic hot-hand paper argued that observers perceive meaningful shooting streaks more often than the evidence justifies, reading random local runs as proof of momentum. This became the canonical basis for treating hot-hand belief as a cognitive fallacy.
findings.source_title: The hot hand in basketball: On the misperception of random sequences

applications.title: Older adults are more susceptible to the hot-hand fallacy in basketball predictions
applications.description: Dr. Alan Castel, a Professor of Psychology at UCLA, tested whether age moderates belief in the hot-hand fallacy. Participants ranging from 22 to 90 years old were told NBA players make about 50% of their shots, then asked whether a player has a better chance of making a shot after making the previous two, and whether it's important to pass to a player on a hot streak. Older participants were significantly more likely to answer yes to both questions than younger participants, suggesting greater reliance on heuristic-based reasoning despite having more lifetime exposure to random sequences.
applications.industry_context: sports psychology / decision-making across the lifespan
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, named researcher's disclosed study on how a cognitive bias varies across the lifespan, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no manipulator or manipulated party, only a finding about who is more susceptible to a specific reasoning error and why.
